clinicalPearls: Cirrhosis is the end stage of many chronic liver injuries: progressive fibrosis disrupts normal architecture and replaces hepatocytes with regenerative nodules; the main etiologic groups are alcohol-associated, chronic viral hepatitis B/C, biliary, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH, formerly NASH), and miscellaneous (cardiac, cryptogenic) (p.2708).
Alcohol-associated cirrhosis is classically micronodular (nodules <3 mm); with abstinence larger nodules may form, giving a mixed micronodular/macronodular pattern (p.2708).
In alcohol-related liver disease the AST is typically higher than the ALT, usually in roughly a 2:1 ratio, and aminotransferases are generally <400 IU/mL (p.2708-2709).

Stigmata of chronic liver disease include scleral icterus, palmar erythema, spider angiomas, parotid enlargement, digital clubbing, muscle wasting, and in men decreased body hair, gynecomastia and testicular atrophy; these are often reversible with abstinence (p.2710).

Portal hypertension is defined as a hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) >5 mmHg; clinically significant portal hypertension is an HVPG >=10 mmHg, carrying substantial risk of decompensation (variceal bleeding, ascites, encephalopathy) (p.2713).

A serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) >=1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension as the cause of ascites; cardiac ascites also shows SAAG >=1.1 g/dL but with ascitic protein >2.5 g/dL, whereas SAAG <1.1 g/dL points to infectious or malignant causes (p.2715).
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed when the ascitic absolute neutrophil count is >250/uL; ascitic protein <1.5 g/dL marks patients at higher risk for SBP (p.2715-2716).
Most common SBP organisms are Escherichia coli and other gut flora; growth of more than two organisms should raise suspicion for secondary peritonitis from a perforated viscus (p.2716).
Hepatorenal syndrome is functional renal failure without renal histopathology; HRS-AKI (old type 1) is rapidly progressive while HRS-CKD (old type 2) is more stable with a better prognosis (p.2716).

In hepatic encephalopathy ammonia is usually elevated, but its level correlates poorly with disease severity, so most hepatologists do not rely on ammonia to diagnose or follow the condition; asterixis (liver flap) is a key bedside sign (p.2716-2717).

Standard PT/INR do not reliably measure clotting capacity in cirrhosis because both pro- and anticoagulant factor synthesis fall (rebalanced hemostasis); adequate thrombin generation occurs at platelet counts above ~50,000-60,000/L (p.2717).

Acute-on-chronic liver failure is acute decompensation of cirrhosis with failure of one or more organ systems, behaves like a sepsis-type systemic inflammatory syndrome, and carries 28-day mortality of roughly 20-70% rising with the number of organ failures (p.2717).
harrison.pathophysiology: Chronic, repeated hepatocellular injury (toxic, viral, immune, metabolic, cholestatic, or congestive) drives Kupffer cell activation and release of profibrogenic cytokines that activate hepatic stellate cells, producing excess collagen and extracellular matrix. Connective tissue links portal triads to central veins, hepatocytes are lost, and regenerative nodules form, so the liver contracts and loses normal architecture - a process taking years to decades. The resulting distorted vasculature raises intrahepatic resistance, which together with splanchnic arterial vasodilation (driven by mediators such as nitric oxide) produces portal hypertension. Splanchnic vasodilation causes effective arterial underfilling, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and sympathetic systems, leading to renal sodium and water retention, plasma volume expansion, and a hyperdynamic circulation; combined with low oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminemia, this generates ascites and edema. Portosystemic shunting plus reduced hepatic mass allows gut-derived neurotoxins (ammonia, false neurotransmitters, mercaptans) to reach the brain and cause encephalopathy (p.2708, p.2713-2717).
additionalDifferentials: Non-cirrhotic portal hypertension (prehepatic portal/splenic vein thrombosis, presinusoidal schistosomiasis or congenital hepatic fibrosis)
Budd-Chiari syndrome and sinusoidal obstruction syndrome as posthepatic outflow causes
Congestive hepatopathy from right-sided heart failure (cardiac cirrhosis)
Cryptogenic cirrhosis later reclassified as burned-out MASH
Infiltrative or malignant liver disease and peritoneal carcinomatosis as alternative causes of ascites
infectionMimics: Schistosomiasis causing presinusoidal portal hypertension that mimics cirrhotic portal hypertension
Chronic viral hepatitis B or C as an underlying driver where the inflammatory/fibrotic picture overlaps with other cirrhosis etiologies
nonInfectiousMimics: Cardiac cirrhosis / congestive hepatopathy from chronic right heart failure
Budd-Chiari syndrome (extravasation of red cells on biopsy helps distinguish from cardiac hepatopathy)
Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (venoocclusive disease) after marrow transplant conditioning or pyrrolizidine alkaloid ingestion
Malignant or cardiac ascites distinguished from cirrhotic ascites by SAAG and ascitic protein
additionalInvestigations: Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic total protein, albumin (for SAAG), cell count with differential, and cultures (inject into blood-culture bottles); amylase and cytology when indicated
Upper GI endoscopy to screen for and characterize gastroesophageal varices and portal hypertensive gastropathy

Etiology workup: HCV RNA and genotype; HBsAg, HBeAg, anti-HBe and HBV DNA; autoimmune markers (ANA, ASMA); iron studies with transferrin saturation/ferritin and HFE testing; ceruloplasmin and 24-h urinary copper; alpha-1 antitrypsin level and phenotype
Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI to show nodular liver and portosystemic collaterals; noninvasive fibrosis tests and, when needed, liver biopsy to confirm cirrhosis
HVPG measurement in selected cases; MRCP (and ERCP if needed) for suspected primary sclerosing cholangitis
DEXA for osteoporosis in cholestatic disease; bubble echocardiography and right-heart catheterization for hepatopulmonary syndrome and portopulmonary hypertension
redFlags: Variceal hemorrhage - immediately life-threatening, with about 20-30% mortality per bleeding episode
New or worsening hepatic encephalopathy, especially with violent agitation or progressive obtundation
Rapidly rising creatinine in a patient with tense ascites suggesting HRS-AKI
Fever, abdominal pain, altered mental status or new AKI in a patient with ascites suggesting SBP
Acute-on-chronic liver failure with multiorgan failure
harrison.prognosis: Severity and bleeding risk are stratified by Child-Pugh class and MELD score. Once clinically significant portal hypertension leads to decompensation, median survival is under 2 years. Less than half of patients survive 2 years after the onset of ascites. Patients with complicated cirrhosis who keep drinking have under 50% 5-year survival, whereas abstinence markedly improves outlook. Development of encephalopathy is a poor prognostic sign, and HRS (AKI or CKD type) carries a poor prognosis without transplantation. ACLF 28-day mortality ranges from roughly 20-70%, rising with the number of failing organs. Liver transplantation is the definitive option for end-stage disease and can reverse HRS (p.2709, p.2713, p.2715-2717).
pitfalls: Relying on PT/INR (or routinely correcting it before procedures) to gauge bleeding risk in cirrhosis - hemostasis is rebalanced and these tests are unreliable
Trusting ammonia levels to diagnose or grade hepatic encephalopathy despite poor correlation with severity
Restricting dietary protein for encephalopathy, which worsens malnutrition and is strongly discouraged
Missing SBP because classic signs may be absent - a high index of suspicion and paracentesis are needed in hospitalized ascitic patients
Using nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides) or unmonitored ACE inhibitors/ARBs in patients with ascites, precipitating renal failure
Forgetting albumin replacement after large-volume paracentesis (>=5 L) to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction
Overlooking sarcopenia masked by obesity or edema in decompensated cirrhosis
harrison.severityClassification: Compensated cirrhosis (HVPG 5-10 mmHg) may be asymptomatic for >=10 years; clinically significant portal hypertension is HVPG >=10 mmHg. Decompensation is marked by variceal bleeding, ascites, or encephalopathy. Overall severity is graded by Child-Pugh class and MELD score, which also predict variceal bleeding risk and guide transplant prioritization. Acute kidney injury is defined as a creatinine rise of 0.3 mg/dL over 48 h or a 50% rise from baseline; SBP is defined by ascitic neutrophils >250/uL (p.2713, p.2715-2716).
management: Treatment of the underlying aetiology, including alcohol abstinence, antiviral therapy for hepatitis B or C, weight loss for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, and immunosuppression for autoimmune hepatitis

Management of ascites with dietary sodium restriction and diuretics such as spironolactone and furosemide, large-volume paracentesis with albumin cover, and consideration of a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt for refractory ascites

Variceal bleeding prophylaxis with a non-selective beta-blocker or endoscopic band ligation, with acute bleeding managed by a vasoactive agent such as terlipressin, prophylactic antibiotics and endoscopic therapy
Hepatic encephalopathy treated with lactulose and rifaximin alongside correction of precipitants
Prompt antibiotics for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis with secondary prophylaxis, plus antibiotic cover after variceal bleeding
Surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma with periodic ultrasound and endoscopic surveillance for varices, alongside nutritional support, vaccination and avoidance of hepatotoxins
Referral for liver transplantation assessment guided by Child-Pugh class and MELD score once decompensation occurs
